text: overview12 of more than 70 randomised studies in 16 000 patients heparin reduced the risk of subclinical DVT by 67% in general surgery, 68% in orthopaedic sur- gery, and 75% in urological surgery. There was also a 40% reduction in non-fatal cases of pulmonary embolism, a 64% reduction in fatal cases, and a 47% reduction of all cases. Surgical thromboembolism prophylaxis with heparin also decreased total mortality. Adjusted-dose heparin may be more effective in higher risk patients but the need for laboratory monitoring and the risk of bleeding complications limit its use. Low-molecular-weight heparins have a number of poten- tial advantages over unfractionated heparin, including less frequent dosage and no need for monitoring, and they are widely used. However, they have not been clearly shown to reduce the risk of bleeding and they may increase the risk of spinal haematoma with spinal or epidural anaesthe- sia, which may limit their use. Generally, studies have shown low-molecular-weight heparins to be as effective as unfractionated or standard heparin, but meta-analyses have come to differing conclusions regarding superiority. 1190 Cardiovascular Drugs The evidence suggests that low-molecular-weight heparins are better in orthopaedic surgery,13-16 particularly with regard to proximal DVT;15 however a systematic review17 concluded that, in patients having surgery for hip fracture, there was not enough evidence to say whether ei- ther is better, or to confirm protection against pulmonary embolism. In general surgery both types of heparin appear to be of equivalent efficacy, although one analysis14 report- ed that low-molecular-weight heparins were superior. A large study18 showed low-molecular-weight heparins to be as effective as heparin for prophylaxis after major abdom- inal surgery and to be associated with fewer bleeding com- plications. UK9 and US11 guidelines suggest that, in gener- al surgery, either may be used. Two meta-analyses of 45 studies19 and 56 studies20 respectively evaluated the effica- cy of several prophylactic methods (such as aspirin, dex- tran, oral anticoagulants, heparin, heparin with dihydroer- gotamine, low-molecular-weight heparins, and intermittent pneumatic compression) against DVT after major hip surgery and concluded that low-molecular- weight heparins should be the method of choice. A meta- analysis21 of low-molecular-weight heparins in major orthopaedic surgery found no evidence that giving the first dose pre- rather than postoperatively was more effective; there were similar risks for major bleeds. Either option is therefore acceptable; first dosage close to the time of sur- gery may be more effective but has been associated with increased risk of major bleeds.
